# SK2174 — The shift or bitwise operand relies on precedence to group

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An operand of `<<`, `>>`, `>>>`, `&`, `|` or `^` is itself an unparenthesised binary expression from a different precedence family, so how the expression groups is a fact about the C# grammar rather than a fact on the page.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

`a << b + 1` shifts by `b + 1`. `mask & offset + 1` masks against `offset + 1`. `a | b & c` is `a | (b & c)`. Every one of those is what the grammar says and none of them is what most readers say when asked, because the shift and bitwise operators sit between arithmetic and comparison in a table nobody has memorised. ⚠ **The parentheses cost nothing and settle it**, which is the whole argument — there is no defect here to find, only a sentence that can be written so it cannot be misread. ⚠ **The boundary against `SK0209` is settled by construction, and settling it was the condition on shipping this at all.** `skala arrange` removes redundant parentheses; `ParenthesesRedundancy.MayRemove` refuses unconditionally when the parent is a shift or a bitwise operator, because `resharper_parentheses_non_obvious_operations` names exactly those. Every pair of parentheses this rule adds has such a parent, so the arranger will never take one back and `skala fix` and `skala arrange --aggressive` cannot fight.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var shifted = value << offset + 1;
```

Write:

```csharp
var shifted = value << (offset + 1);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A closed table, not a heuristic, and three of the rows it was drafted with are gone.** What is reported is one shape: an operand of a shift or bitwise operator that is itself a binary expression of a *different* precedence family, minus one exclusion below. `a & b & c` and `a + b + c` are one family throughout and are never reported; `(a + b) << 1` is already parenthesised and is never reported. ⚠ **A comparison operand under `&` or `|` is declined, and `SK2064` is the reason.** `a & b == c` only compiles when every operand is `bool`, and a `&` between two `bool` operands is `SK2064`'s subject — it reports it and offers `&&`. Reporting it here as well would be two rules on one token. Since arithmetic and shift operands never have `bool` type, the two rules are disjoint by construction: `SK2064` fires only on `bool` operands and this rule only on integral ones. ⚠ **A shift under a bitwise operator is bit packing and is declined, which is the third row measured out.** `key << 8 | digest[i]` and `value << offset & mask` are how every byte of every buffer has ever been assembled, and no reader hesitates: the shift is visibly the thing being placed and the bitwise operator visibly the thing placing it. The rule without that exclusion reports the shape once on Skala's own tree, in `CorpusSample.KeyOf`, and once in `pathological/operators-crammed-together.cs`, and both are the idiom rather than the hazard. What is left is the pair the C precedence table actually catches people out on: arithmetic bound looser than the shift or mask enclosing it, and `&` bound tighter than `^` bound tighter than `|`. ⚠ **The `?:` row was cut because the grammar makes it unreachable.** A conditional expression binds looser than every binary operator, so it can never *be* an unparenthesised binary operand; the only reachable nesting is `a ? b : c ? d : e`, which is the chained-ternary idiom every C# reader parses correctly, and reporting it would be noise. What was drafted as "`?:` inside a larger expression" describes no program. ⚠ **A preprocessor directive inside the operand withdraws the finding**, because a `(` and a `)` inserted on either side of an `#if` do not necessarily both survive into the same compilation. The fix inserts one character at each end of the operand's span and changes nothing else, so it cannot move a comment or reflow a line, which is why it is safe to apply without review. Generated code is excluded.
